etymology: From the Saxon fugelere, a bird-catcher, from fugel, a fowl. It renders the Hebrew yaqosh, one who lays snares — not an archer who shoots the bird openly but a trapper who takes it by concealment.
biblical_def: The fowler is the Bible’s picture of hidden danger, and every detail of his trade preaches. He does not hunt in the open; he sets a snare, conceals it, baits it, and waits, and the bird is taken without ever seeing what took it. So the psalmist’s comfort is aimed exactly where fear lives: “Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence” (Psa 91:3) — the two great terrors of the ancient world being the trap you cannot see and the plague you cannot fight, and God is named as deliverer from both. Solomon urges the same urgency upon a man who has become surety for his neighbour: “Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler” (Pro 6:5) — not negotiate, not delay, but tear yourself loose as a creature already in the hand. Most solemn is Hosea’s indictment, where the fowler is a minister of religion: “the prophet is a snare of a fowler in all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God” (Hos 9:8). The man appointed as watchman to warn of traps has himself become the trap. And the great note of triumph belongs to the escaped: “Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped” (Psa 124:7) — the bird did not break the snare; the snare was broken.
webster_summary: One who takes birds by snares, nets, or lime rather than in open pursuit; in Scripture the standing figure of concealed and patient danger.
webster_full: FOWLER, n. A sportsman who pursues wild fowl, or takes them in nets or snares.
From the Saxon fugelere, from fugel, a fowl or bird.
The fowler’s art lies in concealment and patience rather than in open pursuit.
Rendering the Hebrew yaqosh, to lay a bait or snare.
Figuratively, one who lies in wait to entrap the unwary (Hos 9:8).
scriptures: Psa 91:3
Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence.
Pro 6:5
Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler.
Hos 9:8
The watchman of Ephraim was with my God: but the prophet is a snare of a fowler in all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God.
Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped.
corruption_summary: Temptation is now imagined as an open contest a strong man may safely enter, when Scripture’s figure is a concealed snare which the bird never sees and from which the only wisdom is flight.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the fantasy of the fair fight. Modern men, and modern Christians with them, tend to picture temptation as an opponent to be faced down — a matter of willpower, resolve, and accountability, in which a sufficiently determined man may stand his ground and win. Scripture’s dominant figure says otherwise. The fowler does not challenge the bird; he hides, baits, and waits, and the bird is in the net before it knows a net exists. That is why the Bible’s commands about temptation are so overwhelmingly commands to flee — flee fornication, flee idolatry, flee youthful lusts, flee these things, O man of God. Joseph’s victory was running out of the house without his coat, which looks like defeat and is the only recorded triumph in the chapter.

Recover the plain sense: the snare is concealed, therefore the wisdom is distance rather than valour. Pro 6:5 is a picture of undignified urgency — tear yourself away like a creature already in the hand — and the man who thinks such haste beneath him is the man the fowler is counting on. Add Hosea’s warning that a trap may wear the clothing of a prophet and stand in the house of God, so that the snare is not always in the obvious places. And rest the whole matter on Psa 124:7, which tells you who does the delivering: the snare is broken, and we are escaped. The bird has no power over the net. Its escape is always something done to the net, not by the bird.
roots_summary: Saxon fugelere, a bird-catcher — the trapper who takes by concealment; Scripture’s figure of hidden temptation.
roots_lines: Fowler — Saxon fugelere, from fugel, a bird.
Hebrew yaqosh, to lay a snare or bait.
The trade depends on concealment, bait, and patience — never open pursuit.
Hos 9:8: the prophet himself becomes the fowler’s snare.
Psa 124:7: the snare is broken; the bird does not break it.
usage: The snare is hidden, so Scripture commands flight rather than confrontation.
Pro 6:5 pictures undignified urgency — tear loose as a bird already in the hand.
Psa 124:7 gives the deliverance to God: the snare was broken, not escaped by strength.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s spelling of carcass, from the Old French carcasse, a dead body. It renders the Hebrew nebelah, a thing that has fallen or died of itself, and peger, a corpse — in the law a principal source of ceremonial defilement.
biblical_def: A carcase in Scripture is a dead body, and the law makes it one of the great teachers of uncleanness. Of the unclean beasts it is said, “Of their flesh shall ye not eat, and their carcase shall ye not touch; they are unclean to you” (Lev 11:8), and whosoever toucheth the carcase of them “shall be unclean until the even” (Lev 11:24). Observe the direction of the contagion. Cleanness never spreads by contact; uncleanness always does. Touch a corpse and you become unclean; the corpse does not become clean. That single asymmetry, taught by handling for fifteen centuries, prepared Israel to understand why a Saviour must do more than come near — and why it is astonishing that when Christ touched a leper, the leper was cleansed rather than Christ defiled. The word also carries the bleakest verdict in the wilderness narrative: “Your carcases shall fall in this wilderness” (Num 14:29), which the writer to the Hebrews takes up as a warning to the church — “whose carcases fell in the wilderness” (Heb 3:17). A generation redeemed from Egypt, baptised in the sea, and fed with manna, left as carcases in the sand for unbelief. And there is one strange sweetness: Samson turned aside to the carcase of the lion and found a swarm of bees and honey (Jdg 14:8) — out of the eater came forth meat.
webster_summary: The dead body of an animal or man; in the Mosaic law a chief source of ceremonial defilement, and in the wilderness narrative the mark of a generation that perished in unbelief.
webster_full: CARCASE, CARCASS, n. The dead body of an animal; sometimes of a man, and then in contempt.
From the Old French carcasse; the AV retains the older spelling.
The decaying remains or framework of anything; as, the carcase of a ship.
In the Mosaic law, that which defiles by contact until the even (Lev 11:24).
Rendering the Hebrew nebelah, a body fallen of itself, and peger, a corpse.
scriptures: Lev 11:8
Of their flesh shall ye not eat, and their carcase shall ye not touch; they are unclean to you.
Your carcases shall fall in this wilderness; and all that were numbered of you, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, which have murmured against me,
Jdg 14:8
And after a time he returned to take her, and he turned aside to see the carcase of the lion: and, behold, there was a swarm of bees and honey in the carcase of the lion.
Heb 3:17
But with whom was he grieved forty years? was it not with them that had sinned, whose carcases fell in the wilderness?
corruption_summary: The dietary and contact laws are treated either as primitive hygiene or as arbitrary ritual, when their whole design was to teach by daily handling that defilement spreads and holiness does not.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the reduction of the clean laws to sanitation. It is now a commonplace that Israel’s food and carcase regulations were an early public-health code, thoughtfully given to a people without refrigeration, and that they may be safely retired now that we understand bacteria. This misses the stated ground entirely. The reason given is never health; it is always ye shall be holy, for I am holy. And several of the distinctions make no hygienic sense whatever: the rock badger and the hare are unclean, the locust is clean. The laws were teaching a category, not preventing an illness — drilling into a nation, through the most ordinary daily acts of eating and touching, the difference between clean and unclean, and the direction in which contamination travels.

Recover the plain sense: uncleanness is contagious and cleanness is not, and every Israelite learned this with his hands. That is what makes the Gospels startling. Christ touches the leper and the leper is cleansed; He takes the dead girl by the hand and she rises; the woman with the issue of blood touches His garment and virtue goes out of Him. The flow reverses, and it reverses only in Him. Then hear Heb 3:17 as the warning it is: carcases fell in the wilderness, and they were redeemed carcases — men who had seen the sea open. Deliverance from Egypt did not guarantee entry into Canaan, and profession does not guarantee possession.
roots_summary: Old French carcasse, a dead body — the law’s teacher of defilement, and the wilderness’s verdict on unbelief.
roots_lines: Carcase — the AV spelling of carcass; Old French carcasse.
Hebrew nebelah, a body fallen of itself; peger, a corpse.
Lev 11:24: contact defiles until the even — uncleanness spreads, cleanness does not.
Num 14:29 and Heb 3:17: the carcases of a redeemed generation fell in the sand.
Jdg 14:8: out of the lion’s carcase, honey — out of the eater came forth meat.
usage: The laws teach a category, not a hygiene: ye shall be holy, for I am holy.
In the Gospels the flow reverses — Christ touches the unclean and cleanses.
Heb 3:17 warns the church: redeemed men fell as carcases through unbelief.

etymology: From the Saxon glida, from glidan, to glide — the bird named for its motion, the effortless gliding of a kite upon the wind. It renders the Hebrew raah, a bird of prey, probably a kite or buzzard.
biblical_def: The glede appears once, in the list of birds Israel might not eat: “And the glede, and the kite, and the vulture after his kind” (Deu 14:13). Its English name is a small marvel of old speech — the glider, the bird that hangs on the wind without beating a wing. It stands in a company that repays attention, for nearly every unclean bird in the Levitical catalogue is either a bird of prey or a bird that feeds on carrion: the eagle, the ossifrage, the vulture, the kite, the raven, the owl, the cormorant, the stork, the heron. The principle running through the list is that Israel might not eat the eaters of blood and death. Clean birds are the grain-feeders — the dove, the pigeon, the sparrow, the quail — and it is a clean bird that is offered in sacrifice and a dove that descends upon Christ at His baptism. The distinction thus preached a doctrine at every meal: a people belonging to the living God do not feed upon death. It also preached the doctrine of kinds. The phrase after his kind recurs through the list as it recurs through Gen 1, insisting that God made fixed and separate orders which do not flow into one another. The glede is a small word, but it stands inside a very large argument.
webster_summary: A bird of prey of the kite or buzzard family, named from its gliding flight; one of the fowls forbidden as unclean under the Mosaic law.
webster_full: GLEDE, n. A rapacious bird of the kite kind, so named from its gliding motion.
From the Saxon glida, from glidan, to glide, to move smoothly.
Reckoned among the unclean birds forbidden to the Israelites (Deu 14:13).
Rendering the Hebrew raah, a bird of prey, probably the kite or buzzard.
The forbidden birds are chiefly raptors and carrion-feeders.
scriptures: And the glede, and the kite, and the vulture after his kind,
And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,
And the vulture, and the kite after his kind;
But these are they of which ye shall not eat: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,
corruption_summary: The recurring phrase after his kind in these lists is quietly discarded by the evolutionary account of origins, which the dictionary rejects as contrary to the plain teaching of Gen 1 and of the law that echoes it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the abolition of kinds. The clean and unclean lists repeat after his kind with a persistence that is clearly deliberate, and the phrase reaches back to Gen 1, where God ten times makes creatures after their kind. The evolutionary account requires precisely the opposite: that kinds are not fixed boundaries but temporary appearances in a continuum, every category shading into the next given time enough. The dictionary rejects that account as incompatible with the doctrine of creation the Scriptures actually teach. Whatever variation occurs within a kind — and Scripture never denies variety — the boundaries are God’s work, and it is a settled biblical instinct that what God has distinguished, man must not confuse.

Recover the plain sense: the doctrine of kinds is not an isolated point of natural history but the foundation on which a great deal of biblical ethics is built. The same law that lists the glede after his kind forbids sowing a field with mingled seed, wearing a garment of linen and woollen together, and yoking the ox with the ass. God’s world is a world of distinctions — light from darkness, waters from waters, holy from common, clean from unclean, male from female — and the abolition of one boundary has never long remained the abolition of only one. Meanwhile the plainer lesson stands at the table: a people belonging to the living God do not feed upon death, and the bird that hangs on the wind waiting for a corpse is not the bird that descends upon the Son at His baptism.
roots_summary: Saxon glida, from glidan, to glide — the gliding kite; an unclean bird in a list built on fixed kinds.
roots_lines: Glede — Saxon glida, from glidan, to glide.
Named for its motion: the bird that hangs on the wind without beating a wing.
Hebrew raah, a bird of prey, probably kite or buzzard.
The unclean birds are chiefly raptors and carrion-feeders (Lev 11:13–19).
After his kind recurs through the list as through Gen 1.
usage: Clean birds are grain-feeders; unclean birds feed on blood and death.
It is a clean bird — the dove — that descends upon Christ at His baptism.
After his kind ties the food laws to the doctrine of creation.

etymology: From the Old French hairon, of Germanic origin. A long-legged wading bird of the marsh. It renders the Hebrew anaphah, a word of uncertain identification which some derive from a root signifying to snort or be angry — whence the older suggestion that the bird was named for its irritable temper.
biblical_def: The heron appears twice, in identical company both times: “the stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat” (Lev 11:19; Deu 14:18). It closes the list of unclean fowls, and its habitat is the point. The heron is a bird of the marsh and the standing water, wading in the shallows and feeding on what moves in the mud. Israel’s clean creatures are overwhelmingly creatures of the field and the open pasture; the unclean gather at the edges — the marsh, the ruin, the desert, the night. The distinction is not aesthetic but pedagogical, teaching a people to think in terms of what belongs at the centre and what haunts the margins. The Hebrew name is disputed, and the Authorized Version’s translators, faced with an uncertain bird, gave an honest English equivalent rather than a transliteration — which is itself worth noticing at a time when their scholarship is often disparaged. They marked their uncertainty in the margin elsewhere and did not pretend to more than they had. The phrase after her kind attaches here as through the whole list, and reminds the reader that these are not individual species arbitrarily banned but whole orders of creature, fixed by the God who made them and distinguished by the God who chose Israel.
webster_summary: A long-legged wading bird of the marshes, numbered among the unclean fowls of the Mosaic law.
webster_full: HERON, n. A large wading fowl with long legs and neck, frequenting marshes and the margins of rivers.
From the Old French hairon; of Germanic origin.
Reckoned unclean under the law of Moses (Lev 11:19; Deu 14:18).
Rendering the Hebrew anaphah, a bird not certainly identified.
Some derive the Hebrew from a root signifying to be angry or to snort.
scriptures: And the stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat.
And the stork, and the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat.
This is the law of the beasts, and of the fowl, and of every living creature that moveth in the waters, and of every creature that creepeth upon the earth:
To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.
corruption_summary: Uncertainty over a few Hebrew bird-names is regularly inflated into a general charge that the Authorized Version is unreliable — a conclusion the evidence does not carry.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the argument from a hard case to a general verdict. Because anaphah cannot be identified with modern zoological certainty, and because translators have rendered it heron, cormorant, or plover, it is urged that the whole translation stands on sand and that ordinary readers cannot trust the text before them. The inference is far larger than the evidence. A handful of rare nouns — certain birds, gems, and plants named once or twice in a dead language — are genuinely uncertain, and every honest version says so. Not one doctrine of the Christian faith rests upon any of them. The clean and unclean lists preach exactly the same lesson whichever marsh bird anaphah names.

Recover the plain sense: the difficulty is real, small, and honestly handled. The translators of 1611 did not conceal such places; they used the margin freely to note alternatives, which is the mark of workmen who feared God more than they feared looking uncertain. That is the proper posture for readers too. Where Scripture is plain it binds the conscience absolutely; where a rare word is obscure, the obscurity is confessed and no weight is hung upon it. What is perfectly plain in Lev 11 is the doctrine: God distinguishes, His people must distinguish, and the ground of the whole chapter is stated in its own words — to put difference between the unclean and the clean.
roots_summary: Old French hairon, a marsh wader — an unclean bird of the margins; a rare Hebrew name honestly rendered.
roots_lines: Heron — Old French hairon, of Germanic origin.
Hebrew anaphah, a bird not certainly identified.
Listed with the stork, the lapwing, and the bat (Lev 11:19).
A creature of the marsh and standing water — the unclean haunt the margins.
Lev 11:47: the chapter’s own stated purpose is to put difference between clean and unclean.
usage: The unclean birds gather at the margins — marsh, ruin, desert, and night.
The 1611 translators marked genuine uncertainty rather than inventing precision.
No doctrine rests on the identification of a rare bird-name.

etymology: From the Greek satyros, the goat-formed woodland demon of the heathen poets, through the Latin satyrus. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew sair, literally “hairy one,” the ordinary word for a he-goat, used in Isaiah of the creatures that haunt a ruined place.
biblical_def: The satyrs appear in the two great desolation-oracles of Isaiah. Of fallen Babylon: “wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there” (Isa 13:21). Of ruined Edom: “the satyr shall cry to his fellow” (Isa 34:14). The Hebrew sair means a shaggy or hairy one and is the common word for a he-goat; the same word is used of the goat-idols Israel was forbidden to sacrifice unto, “after whom they have gone a whoring” (Lev 17:7). This double use is the key to the passages. Isaiah is describing cities so utterly overthrown that nothing remains but wild goats capering in the ruins — and, with a grim irony, the very creatures whose images the nations worshipped now inhabit the empty temples of their worshippers. The demon-goats have the place to themselves at last. Whether Isaiah intends literal wild goats or the heathen’s own imagined demons, the prophetic point is identical and devastating: what a nation worships, it is finally left alone with. The proud city that would not have God ends as a dance-floor for goats, and Isa 34:14 lets you hear it — one shaggy creature calling to another across the silence where a kingdom stood.
webster_summary: In the Authorized Version, the shaggy or goat-like creature said to haunt a desolated place; the Hebrew word is the ordinary term for a he-goat, and is also used of the goat-idols of the heathen.
webster_full: SATYR, n. In mythology, a sylvan deity or demigod, represented as a monster, half man and half goat.
From the Greek satyros; Latin satyrus.
In Scripture, rendering the Hebrew sair, a hairy one, the common word for a he-goat.
The same Hebrew is used of goat-idols to which Israel sacrificed (Lev 17:7; 2Ch 11:15).
Used by Isaiah of the creatures inhabiting Babylon and Edom after their overthrow.
scriptures: But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there.
The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; the screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest.
Lev 17:7
And they shall no more offer their sacrifices unto devils, after whom they have gone a whoring. This shall be a statute for ever unto them throughout their generations.
And he ordained him priests for the high places, and for the devils, and for the calves which he had made.
corruption_summary: The passage is used in two opposite errors — treated by sceptics as proof that Scripture believed in pagan demigods, and by the sensational as a demonology text — when Isaiah’s point is that a city ends inhabited by what it worshipped.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption runs in two directions, and both mistake the genre. The sceptic points to the satyrs and announces that the Bible shares the superstitions of its neighbours, populating ruins with goat-demons exactly as the Greek poets did. That misreads a Hebrew word: sair is the plain term for a he-goat, and Isaiah is describing a desolation so complete that livestock run wild through the streets. In the other direction, sensational writers build elaborate demonologies on these verses, mapping hierarchies of ruin-dwelling spirits from two poetic lines in an oracle against Babylon. Scripture gives no such system, and a doctrine of the unseen world assembled out of prophetic imagery is a house built on figures of speech.

Recover the plain sense: this is judgment poetry, and its argument is exact. Israel had sacrificed to the seirim, the goat-idols, and gone a whoring after them (Lev 17:7); Jeroboam appointed priests for them at Bethel (2Ch 11:15). Isaiah now shows the nations left alone with those same shaggy creatures dancing in their emptied cities. That is how God commonly judges idolatry — not by destroying the idol first, but by granting a people undisturbed possession of it. He gave them up, says Paul three times over in Romans 1. The most terrible thing that can befall a city is to be handed over to exactly what it wanted, and to hear nothing at last but one goat crying to his fellow.
roots_summary: Greek satyros, rendering Hebrew sair, a hairy one or he-goat — the creature left dancing in a city that worshipped it.
roots_lines: Satyr — Greek satyros, the goat-formed woodland demon of the poets.
Hebrew sair, a hairy one; the ordinary word for a he-goat.
The same word names the goat-idols of Lev 17:7 and 2Ch 11:15.
Isa 13:21 and 34:14 place them in the ruins of Babylon and Edom.
The irony is deliberate: the worshipped creature inherits the worshipper’s city.
usage: Read as judgment poetry, not as a demonology; no system should be built on it.
Lev 17:7 shows Israel sacrificing to the seirim — the same word.
The judgment is abandonment: a people left alone with what they chose.

etymology: From the Greek pygargos — pyge, the rump, and argos, white — literally “white-rump.” The Authorized Version takes the name from the Septuagint, which so rendered the Hebrew dishon, a clean wild animal, probably a species of antelope or addax.
biblical_def: The pygarg occurs once, in the list of beasts Israel might eat: “The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois” (Deu 14:5). Its name is a small window into how the Authorized Version was made. The Hebrew dishon was already obscure by the third century before Christ, and the Jewish translators of the Septuagint rendered it pygargos — the white-rumped creature, a description of the animal’s most visible field mark, which is how herdsmen everywhere name animals they know by sight. Our translators, working centuries later on the same difficult word, kept the ancient identification rather than inventing a new one. The verse itself belongs to the generous side of the law, which is easily forgotten. Deu 14 is commonly remembered for what it forbade; verse 5 is a list of what a free Israelite might hunt on the hills and eat without ceremony — seven wild creatures, taken by any man with a bow, needing no priest and no altar. God’s law fenced His people about with restrictions, and it also set a table for them in the open country. The pygarg is a reminder that the same chapter which says thou shalt not eat says at greater length these ye shall eat.
webster_summary: A clean wild animal named in the Mosaic law, probably an antelope or addax; the name is Greek for “white-rump,” taken from the Septuagint.
webster_full: PYGARG, PYGARGUS, n. A kind of wild animal reckoned clean under the Mosaic law.
From the Greek pygargos, from pyge, the rump, and argos, white.
Rendering the Hebrew dishon, a creature not certainly identified; probably the addax or a species of antelope.
Named among the beasts the Israelites were permitted to eat (Deu 14:5).
The name is descriptive, taken from the animal’s conspicuous white hindquarters.
scriptures: Deu 14:4
These are the beasts which ye shall eat: the ox, the sheep , and the goat,
Deu 14:5
The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois.
Deu 14:6
And every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat.

Notwithstanding thou mayest kill and eat flesh in all thy gates, whatsoever thy soul lusteth after, according to the blessing of the LORD thy God which he hath given thee: the unclean and the clean may eat thereof, as of the roebuck, and as of the hart.
corruption_summary: The law is remembered almost entirely as prohibition, so a chapter that names seven wild creatures an Israelite might freely hunt and eat is read as though it were only a list of restrictions.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The distortion is one of emphasis, and it runs deep. Ask most people, believer or not, what the law of Moses was about, and the answer will be a catalogue of things forbidden. Deu 14 is a fair test of that impression. It does forbid; but verses 4 to 6 name the ox, the sheep, the goat, the hart, the roebuck, the fallow deer, the wild goat, the pygarg, the wild ox, and the chamois, and Deu 12:15 adds that a man may kill and eat flesh in all his gates, whatsoever his soul lusteth after, the unclean and the clean alike eating of it as of the roebuck and the hart. That is a wide liberty, granted in plain words, and it is not the picture of God most people carry.

Recover the plain sense: the boundaries in Scripture are always drawn around a garden, not around a desert. In Eden the first word was of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat, and the prohibition concerned one tree. The serpent’s method was to reverse the proportions — hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree? — making the single restriction appear to be the whole arrangement. That remains his method. A man persuaded that God’s law is essentially a list of denials will obey it, if at all, as a slave; a man who sees the hills full of harts and pygargs he is free to take will keep the few boundaries as a son.
roots_summary: Greek pyge + argos, white-rump — a clean wild beast of Deu 14:5, named by its field mark.
roots_lines: Pygarg — Greek pygargos, from pyge, rump, and argos, white.
Taken by the AV from the Septuagint’s rendering of Hebrew dishon.
Probably the addax or a related antelope of the desert.
One of seven wild creatures Israel was free to hunt and eat (Deu 14:5).
Deu 12:15 grants a wide liberty: eat in all thy gates, clean and unclean alike.
usage: Deu 14:4–6 is a list of permissions, not prohibitions.
The name is descriptive — herdsmen name animals by their visible marks.
Scripture’s boundaries are drawn around a garden, not a desert.

etymology: From the Greek dromas, running, through the Late Latin dromedarius — the running camel. Not a distinct species but the swift riding breed, as a courser is to a cart-horse; bred for speed and used for couriers and for flight.
biblical_def: The dromedary is the racing camel, and Jeremiah turns it into one of the most withering images in the prophets. Judah protests her innocence — “How canst thou say, I am not polluted, I have not gone after Baalim?” — and the answer is to point at the tracks: “see thy way in the valley, know what thou hast done: thou art a swift dromedary traversing her ways” (Jer 2:23). The picture is of a young she-camel in heat, running frantically in every direction, crossing and recrossing her own trail, so that the whole valley is written over with the evidence of her wandering. The denial is refuted not by argument but by footprints. And the next verse presses harder still, comparing her to the wild ass in her season, “in her occasion who can turn her away?” (Jer 2:24) — the appetite is now beyond restraint, and any who seek her need not weary themselves; in her month they shall find her. That is the doctrine of habitual sin stated without mercy: the sinner who says I am not polluted has left a record in the dust that answers him, and the appetite he indulged has become an appetite he no longer governs. Elsewhere the beast appears in its ordinary honour, among the swift camels of Midian bearing gold and incense (Isa 60:6) and carrying the king’s posts in Esther.
webster_summary: A swift breed of camel used for riding and couriers rather than burden; in Jeremiah, the figure of an appetite running uncontrolled and leaving its own evidence.
webster_full: DROMEDARY, n. A species or rather variety of camel, bred and used for swiftness.
From the Greek dromas, running, from dramein, to run; Late Latin dromedarius.
Distinguished from the common camel as a courser is from a cart-horse; used for riding and dispatch.
Employed for royal posts and messengers (Est 8:10).
Figuratively, of ungoverned and restless appetite (Jer 2:23).
scriptures: Jer 2:23
How canst thou say, I am not polluted, I have not gone after Baalim? see thy way in the valley, know what thou hast done: thou art a swift dromedary traversing her ways;
Jer 2:24

A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure ; in her occasion who can turn her away? all they that seek her will not weary themselves; in her month they shall find her.
Isa 60:6
The multitude of camels shall cover thee, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; all they from Sheba shall come: they shall bring gold and incense; and they shall shew forth the praises of the LORD.
Est 8:10
And he wrote in the king Ahasuerus' name, and sealed it with the king's ring, and sent letters by posts on horseback, and riders on mules, camels, and young dromedaries:
corruption_summary: Self-justification is the standing reflex of the age — I am not polluted — and Jeremiah answers it not with argument but by pointing at the tracks a life has left.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the sincere denial. Judah does not say I sinned and it does not matter; she says I have not gone after Baalim, and she appears to believe it. This is the most dangerous condition a soul can be in, and it is the characteristic condition of a therapeutic age which has been trained to consult its feelings for a verdict on its conduct. If a man does not feel polluted, he concludes he is not, and the introspection that was supposed to produce honesty produces only a more confident self-acquittal. Jeremiah refuses to argue on that ground at all. He does not ask Judah how she feels; he says see thy way in the valley — look at the trail you have actually left.

Recover the plain sense: conduct is evidence, and a life leaves tracks that can be read. This is the same method the Apostle John uses when he says he that doeth righteousness is righteous, and the same our Lord uses when He says by their fruits ye shall know them. It is a mercy, because it gives the anxious believer something outside his own shifting feelings to examine, and it is a terror to the self-deceived, because the valley keeps a record his memory has edited. Note also Jer 2:24: what begins as a choice ends as a compulsion, an appetite that who can turn away? The way back is not a better opinion of oneself but the confession Judah would not make.
roots_summary: Greek dromas, running — the swift riding camel; in Jeremiah, appetite running uncontrolled and leaving its own record.
roots_lines: Dromedary — Greek dromas, running; Late Latin dromedarius.
Not a separate species but the swift breed, used for riding and dispatch.
The same root gives hippodrome and aerodrome, places of running.
Jer 2:23: a young she-camel crossing and recrossing her own tracks.
Est 8:10: employed to carry the king’s posts with speed.
usage: Jer 2:23 answers a sincere denial with physical evidence: see thy way in the valley.
Jer 2:24 shows appetite passing from choice into compulsion.
Conduct is evidence — the same test as by their fruits ye shall know them.

etymology: From the Saxon milc, milk — the adjectival form, meaning giving milk, in milk. Applied to a cow, camel, or goat currently nursing young, and therefore to a beast at its most valuable and least willing to be separated from its calf.
biblical_def: Milch means giving milk, and the word carries the whole weight of one of the strangest tests in Scripture. The Philistines, tormented by the ark they had captured, resolved to send it back and devised an experiment to learn whether their plagues were from the God of Israel or mere chance: “make a new cart, and take two milch kine, on which there hath come no yoke, and tie the kine to the cart, and bring their calves home from them” (1Sa 6:7). Every element was chosen to make the natural outcome certain. The cows had never been yoked, so they should have fought the harness; they were nursing, so every instinct should have dragged them back toward the calves shut up at home; no driver led them. If they went straight toward Bethshemesh, only God could be moving them. “And the kine took the straight way to the way of Bethshemesh, and went along the highway, lowing as they went, and turned not aside to the right hand or to the left” (1Sa 6:12). That detail — lowing as they went — is one of the most affecting in the Old Testament. The beasts obeyed and grieved at once, crying for their calves the whole way and never turning. Even the Philistine lords could draw the conclusion. The word appears again in Jacob’s present to Esau, “thirty milch camels with their colts” (Gen 32:15), the costliest item in a costly gift.
webster_summary: Giving milk; in milk. Applied to a cow, camel, or goat nursing young, and so to a beast at the height of its value and least willing to leave its calf.
webster_full: MILCH, adj. Giving milk; as, a milch cow.
From the Saxon milc, milk; the adjectival form now nearly obsolete except in this phrase.
Applied to kine, camels, and goats in the season of nursing.
A milch beast was reckoned among the most valuable of a man’s stock (Gen 32:15).
1Sa 6:7 turns the natural instinct of a milch cow into the terms of a divine test.
scriptures: Thirty milch camels with their colts, forty kine, and ten bulls, twenty she asses, and ten foals.
Now therefore make a new cart, and take two milch kine, on which there hath come no yoke, and tie the kine to the cart, and bring their calves home from them:
And the men did so; and took two milch kine, and tied them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home:

And the kine took the straight way to the way of Bethshemesh, and went along the highway , lowing as they went, and turned not aside to the right hand or to the left; and the lords of the Philistines went after them unto the border of Bethshemesh.
corruption_summary: The account is dismissed as folklore because it turns on animal behaviour, when the Philistines designed it precisely so that ordinary animal behaviour would give the answer — and it is a rebuke to a church that will not obey while grieving.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation the passage exposes is the notion that obedience and sorrow cannot occupy the same road. Christians frequently suppose that if a duty grieves them, they have not truly submitted; that a right decision made with tears is somehow a lesser obedience than a right decision made gladly. The kine of Bethshemesh answer that. They went straight, and they lowed the whole way. Their grief was real, their calves were genuinely behind them, and the lowing never became a turning. Nowhere does the narrative suggest their crying spoiled the obedience — it is recorded as part of the miracle, and the lords of the Philistines followed after them to the border.

Recover the plain sense: God does not require that His people cease to feel the cost of what He asks. Abraham climbed Moriah in three days of silence; the Lord Himself prayed that the cup might pass and then drank it; and Paul took the road to Jerusalem with the brethren weeping and breaking his heart, saying the will of the Lord be done. Set that against the counterfeit standard, which measures obedience by cheerfulness and so tempts the grieving saint to think himself a hypocrite. The test is direction, not emotion. Go straight, and low as you go.
roots_summary: Saxon milc, milk — giving milk; the nursing beast whose instinct made the Philistines’ test decisive.
roots_lines: Milch — Saxon milc, milk; the adjective, meaning in milk.
Applied to kine, camels, and goats nursing their young.
Gen 32:15: thirty milch camels, the costliest part of Jacob’s present.
1Sa 6:7: unyoked and nursing — every instinct set against the journey.
1Sa 6:12: they went straight, lowing as they went, and turned not aside.
usage: The test was designed so that ordinary instinct would give a clear answer.
Lowing as they went: grief and obedience travelling the same road.
The measure of obedience is direction, not cheerfulness.

etymology: From the Saxon cote, a small house, hut, or shelter — the same word that survives in dovecote, sheepcote, and the surname Cotes. A cote is a modest enclosure for animals, not a stable or a palace.
biblical_def: Cotes appears once, in the inventory of Hezekiah’s wealth: “Storehouses also for the increase of corn, and wine, and oil; and stalls for all manner of beasts, and cotes for flocks” (2Ch 32:28). The verse belongs to a passage of unusual honesty about a good king. Hezekiah had just been delivered from Sennacherib and healed of a mortal sickness, and God gave him “exceeding much riches and honour” — treasuries for silver and gold, spices, shields, and these humble sheepcotes for his flocks. Then comes the sentence that turns the chapter: “But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up” (2Ch 32:25). The prosperity that followed his deliverance proved more dangerous to him than the Assyrian army. He survived the siege and nearly failed the blessing. The chronicler adds a remarkable comment on the visit of the Babylonian ambassadors, that God “left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart” (2Ch 32:31) — the trial was not to inform God but to show Hezekiah himself what the siege had never revealed. The word cotes is a small domestic detail, and it sits inside one of Scripture’s clearest warnings that deliverance is not the end of a man’s testing but frequently the beginning of a harder one.
webster_summary: Small shelters or enclosures for sheep and other flocks; humble outbuildings, as distinguished from stalls or stables.
webster_full: COTE, n. A sheepfold; a shed or enclosure for beasts; a small house or hut.
From the Saxon cote, a cottage or hut; the root of cottage.
Surviving in dovecote and sheepcote (2Sa 7:8).
Distinguished from stalls, which are for the greater cattle (2Ch 32:28).
In the plural, cotes, the folds belonging to a great man’s estate.
scriptures: And Hezekiah had exceeding much riches and honour: and he made himself treasuries for silver, and for gold, and for precious stones, and for spices, and for shields, and for all manner of pleasant jewels;
Storehouses also for the increase of corn, and wine, and oil; and stalls for all manner of beasts, and cotes for flocks.
But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up: therefore there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem.

Howbeit in the business of the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, who sent unto him to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land, God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart.
corruption_summary: Prosperity is widely read as the seal of God’s approval, when the chronicler places Hezekiah’s storehouses and cotes immediately beside the note that his heart was lifted up.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the prosperity reading of providence, and 2Ch 32 dismantles it from the inside. The chapter grants everything the prosperity teacher wants: a godly king, a miraculous deliverance, a healing from certain death, and then riches and honour in exceeding measure, explicitly given by God. And in the middle of the inventory the chronicler sets the ruin — Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up. The blessing was real and the pride was real, and the second grew directly out of the first. The dictionary rejects the doctrine that material increase is evidence of divine favour toward a man’s soul. It may equally be the arena of his sharpest trial.

Recover the plain sense: the danger of blessing is that it removes the felt necessity of God. Hezekiah on the wall with the Assyrian host below him spread a letter before the LORD and prayed one of the great prayers of Scripture; Hezekiah among his treasuries showed the Babylonians everything he owned and asked God nothing. Note the chronicler’s astonishing explanation — God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart. The trial was diagnostic, and the patient was the one who needed the diagnosis. A man may learn more about himself from a full storehouse than from a siege, and what he learns is rarely flattering.
roots_summary: Saxon cote, a hut or shelter — humble folds for flocks; part of the prosperity that tried Hezekiah harder than Sennacherib did.
roots_lines: Cotes — Saxon cote, a hut, shed, or small enclosure.
The same word gives cottage, dovecote, and sheepcote.
Distinguished from stalls, which housed the greater cattle.
2Ch 32:28 lists them among Hezekiah’s God-given riches.
2Ch 32:25 immediately adds that his heart was lifted up.
usage: The cotes sit in an inventory of blessing that becomes a warning within three verses.
2Ch 32:31: God left him to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart.
Hezekiah survived the siege and nearly failed the prosperity.

etymology: From the Old French covert, the past participle of covrir, to cover — Latin cooperire. A covert is a covered place: a thicket, a shelter, a hiding place. The modern sense of secret is a later development from the same root.
biblical_def: A covert is a covered place, and Scripture uses it for every kind of shelter from the mildest to the most exalted. It is a feature of the landscape: Abigail came down “by the covert of the hill” (1Sa 25:20), riding to meet David with her loaves and her wisdom just where the ground hid her approach. It is a piece of temple architecture — “the covert for the sabbath that they had built in the house” (2Ki 16:18), which Ahaz stripped away for the king of Assyria, a small sentence recording a large apostasy. It is a duty owed to refugees: “Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler” (Isa 16:4). And it rises to its great uses in the mouth of faith. The psalmist says, “I will trust in the covert of thy wings” (Psa 61:4), taking shelter not under a hill but under God Himself. Isaiah promises a tabernacle “for a covert from storm and from rain” (Isa 4:6), and then makes the covert a man: “a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest” (Isa 32:2). That is the word’s destination. The shelter Israel needed was finally not a thicket, a roof, or a wing, but a Person — and He stands in the open weather Himself to be one.
webster_summary: A covered or sheltering place: a thicket, a shelter from storm, a hiding place. Used of landscape, of architecture, of the wings of God, and at last of a man.
webster_full: COVERT, n. A covering, shelter, or defense; a place of protection.
A thicket; a shady place; a hiding place for game.
From the Old French covert, past participle of covrir, to cover; Latin cooperire.
COVERT, adj. Covered; hid; secret; disguised — a later sense of the same word.
In Scripture, a shelter from storm, tempest, or the face of the spoiler (Isa 4:6; Isa 16:4).
scriptures: And it was so, as she rode on the ass, that she came down by the covert of the hill, and, behold, David and his men came down against her; and she met them.
Psa 61:4
I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings. Selah.
Isa 4:6
And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain.
Isa 32:2
And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.
corruption_summary: Isa 32:2 is regularly softened into a promise that Christ shelters us from difficulty, when the verse describes a man who becomes a covert by standing in the weather himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the sheltered-life reading. Isa 32:2 is a favourite verse for consolation, and it is commonly preached as though it promised that the Christian, being in Christ, will be kept out of the wind and the tempest altogether. The grammar will not bear it. The verse says a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind — the shelter is a person, and a person who shelters others is by definition standing in what they are sheltered from. The wind does not stop; it is intercepted. Read the chapter and this becomes plain: the promise is given to a people who will still know storm, and the mercy offered is not the abolition of weather but a covert in the middle of it.

Recover the plain sense: Christ is the man of Isa 32:2, and the cross is what it costs to be a hiding place. He was not spared the wind; He met it, and the darkness at noon was the tempest breaking on Him rather than on His people. That truth also converts the verse into a pattern for His servants. A pastor, a father, a friend who intends to be a covert to anyone must expect to stand where the weather is, and the measure of the shelter he gives will be the measure of what strikes him instead. Set beside it Psa 61:4 and Isa 16:4, and the duty is complete — hide yourself under the wings of God, and be a covert to the outcast at your own door.
roots_summary: Old French covert, covered — a sheltering place; from thicket and wing to the Man who is a covert from the tempest.
roots_lines: Covert — Old French covert, past participle of covrir, to cover.
Latin cooperire, to cover over; the adjectival sense secret is later.
Of landscape: the covert of the hill (1Sa 25:20).
Of God: the covert of thy wings (Psa 61:4).
Of a man: a covert from the tempest (Isa 32:2) — shelter by interception.
usage: Isa 32:2 makes the shelter a Person standing in the weather, not a removal from it.
Isa 16:4 makes providing covert to the outcast a duty laid even upon Moab.
2Ki 16:18: Ahaz removed the sabbath covert for the king of Assyria — apostasy in a detail.
